TUOL SLENG, Cambodia (CNN)  -- The trial of a former prison chief with the Khmer Rouge movement resumed inside a packed Cambodian courtroom Monday, with prosecutors painting a grim picture of inmates who were electrocuted, whipped and beaten to death. Duch ran a prison where people were tortured and killed under the Khmer Rouge. Kaing Guek Eav, a former math teacher and a born-again Christian, displayed no emotion as the U.N.-backed tribunal accused him not just of overseeing the torture and killing of more than 15,000 men, women and children three decades ago -- but of actively taking part in some of them. The trial of the 66-year-old man, better known as Duch, resumed Monday just outside the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh. Spectators, many of them survivors of the abuse, watched the proceedings from an auditorium separated from the courtroom by a large glass window. The proceedings began with Duch offering a basic introduction of himself. Court officials then read out the findings of their lengthy investigation. Prosecutors contend Duch ran S-21, a prison that had been converted from a school. Here, men, women and children were shackled to iron beds and tortured -- before they were beaten to death, prosecutors said. Many of the victims were military officials or Communist Party members targeted for not going along with the philosophy of the ultra-Maoist Khmer Rouge movement, prosecutors said. Duch faces charges that include crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture and murder. He has admitted his role in the Khmer Rouge's genocidal reign.  Watch why his trial is significant » . The movement swept to power in 1975. Three years, eight months and 20 days later, at least 1.7 million people -- nearly one-quarter of Cambodia's population -- were dead from execution, disease, starvation and overwork, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. The non-profit organization has been at the forefront of recording the atrocities committed during the Khmer Rouge regime. S-21 was one of 189 similar institutions across Cambodia. Duch is the first former Khmer Rouge leader to stand trial. The tribunal, which is made up of Cambodian and international judges, does not have the power to impose the death penalty. If convicted, Duch faces from five years to life in prison. The trial is expected to last three or four months. "Probably the most important thing about this court is: even after 35 years, you are still not going to get away with it. That is the message," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit. Even though Duch was not a senior leader with the movement, many Cambodians were relieved that one of the regime's former leaders was facing justice, said Youk Chhang, head of the Documentation Center of Cambodia. "I think there is a feeling of, well you know, finally -- now it's finally happening after all these years of waiting -- hearing, fighting, negotiating," he told CNN last month. "People have that kind of sense of relief that it's now moving. When I ask people around the center today, people say, 'Oh, it's about time.'" Four of the regime's former leaders, also accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, await trial before the tribunal. The regime's leader, Pol Pot, died in 1998. "It all seems so fresh," said Norng Champhal, who was a starving little boy when Vietnamese forces invaded the prison. He was separated from his mother after a night in the prison and never saw her again. "It's hard to control my feelings when I see this," he said, as he watched footage of the prison taken 30 years ago. "I wonder whether my parents were tortured like these people," he said. CNN's Dan Rivers contributed to this report.

**TUOL SLENG, Cambodia (CNN) —** Proceedings against a former Khmer Rouge prison commander continued Monday in a crowded Cambodian court, where prosecutors described prisoners being shocked with electricity, lashed, and fatally beaten.

Kaing Guek Eav—widely known as Duch—was in charge of a detention center where the Khmer Rouge tortured and executed people. The former mathematics teacher, who later became a born-again Christian, showed no visible reaction as the United Nations-supported tribunal alleged that he had both supervised and personally participated in some of the torture and killings of more than 15,000 men, women, and children roughly 30 years earlier.

The trial of Duch, 66, resumed at a court outside Phnom Penh, Cambodia’s capital. A large audience, including many survivors of Khmer Rouge abuse, observed from a hall divided from the courtroom by a broad glass partition.

Duch began the session by briefly identifying himself. Court personnel then presented the conclusions of an extensive investigation.

According to prosecutors, Duch directed S-21, a former school transformed into a prison. Men, women, and children were chained to metal beds and tortured there before being beaten to death. Prosecutors said many prisoners were military personnel or members of the Communist Party who were suspected of failing to support the ideology of the extreme Maoist Khmer Rouge.

Duch was charged with offenses including murder, torture, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. He acknowledged his involvement in the Khmer Rouge’s genocidal rule.

The Khmer Rouge seized control of Cambodia in 1975. By the time its rule ended three years, eight months, and 20 days later, at least 1.7 million people—almost one-fourth of the country’s population—had died through executions, illness, hunger, and forced labor, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. The nonprofit group has played a leading role in documenting crimes committed under the regime.

S-21 was one of 189 comparable facilities operating throughout Cambodia. Duch became the first former Khmer Rouge official to be tried.

The tribunal consists of judges from Cambodia and other countries, and it cannot issue a death sentence. A conviction could bring Duch a prison term ranging from five years to life. The proceedings were expected to continue for three to four months.

Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit said the court’s central message was that perpetrators could still be held accountable even after 35 years.

Although Duch had not belonged to the Khmer Rouge’s highest leadership ranks, many Cambodians felt reassured that a former regime figure was finally being brought before a court, said Youk Chhang, director of the Documentation Center of Cambodia.

Speaking to CNN the previous month, Chhang said people felt that justice was at last moving forward after years of waiting, testimony, disputes, and negotiations. He added that staff members at the center commonly reacted by saying the trial was long overdue.

Four other former Khmer Rouge leaders, accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, were awaiting their own trials before the same tribunal. Pol Pot, who led the regime, died in 1998.

Norng Champhal, who had been a severely underfed young boy when Vietnamese troops entered the prison, said the memories still felt immediate. After spending a night at the facility, he was separated from his mother and never saw her again.

While viewing film of the prison recorded 30 years earlier, Champhal said he struggled to contain his emotions and wondered whether his parents had endured the same torture shown in the footage.

CNN’s Dan Rivers contributed to the report.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary name, Duch, became the first senior Khmer Rouge figure to stand trial before Cambodia’s U.N.-backed war crimes tribunal. As commandant of Security Prison 21, or S-21, in Phnom Penh, he oversaw one of the regime’s most notorious detention and interrogation centers. Between 1975 and 1979, more than 15,000 men, women, and children were imprisoned there, photographed, tortured, and forced to make confessions before being executed, often at the nearby Choeung Ek killing fields. Only a small number of prisoners are known to have survived.

Prosecutors alleged that Duch did more than administer the prison. He trained and supervised interrogators, approved torture, maintained detailed records, and helped ensure that detainees were ultimately killed. Former prisoners, relatives of victims, and ex-Khmer Rouge personnel gave testimony about the prison’s brutal conditions and systematic violence. The surviving photographs, confessions, and execution lists from S-21 provided extensive documentary evidence of the crimes committed there.

During the proceedings, Duch admitted his involvement and accepted responsibility for many of the atrocities carried out under his authority. He expressed remorse and asked victims and their families for forgiveness, although the sincerity and legal significance of his statements remained contested. He was prosecuted for war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as torture and murder under Cambodian law.

The trial represented a historic step in Cambodia’s long and difficult effort to confront the legacy of the Khmer Rouge. Led by Pol Pot, the regime sought to transform the country into an agrarian communist society, emptying cities, abolishing money and private property, separating families, and subjecting the population to forced labor, starvation, persecution, and execution. At least 1.7 million people died from violence, hunger, disease, and overwork during its rule.

For many Cambodians, Duch’s prosecution came decades too late, after years of civil conflict, political compromise, and delays in establishing the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia. Nevertheless, the case marked the first time a major official of the Khmer Rouge was held publicly accountable in a court of law. It also created an official record of the suffering endured at S-21 and gave survivors and victims’ families an opportunity to testify about crimes that had shaped Cambodia for generations.

## Tuol Sleng, Cambodia

Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum in Phnom Penh is one of Cambodia’s most important memorial sites. The building was originally a secondary school, but after the Khmer Rouge seized power in 1975, it was transformed into Security Prison 21, commonly known as S-21.

Between 1975 and 1979, thousands of prisoners were detained, interrogated, and tortured at Tuol Sleng. Many were forced to make false confessions before being transported to the Choeung Ek killing fields, where they were executed. Only a small number of prisoners are known to have survived.

Today, Tuol Sleng preserves prison cells, photographs, documents, and personal testimonies. These exhibits reveal both the systematic nature of the Khmer Rouge regime’s crimes and the individual lives behind the statistics. The museum is not only a place of mourning but also a center for education and remembrance.

Visiting Tuol Sleng can be emotionally difficult, yet it offers essential insight into Cambodia’s recent history. By preserving evidence and honoring the victims, the museum reminds future generations of the consequences of political extremism, dehumanization, and unchecked violence.

counterfactuals.output:
**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (CNN) —** The trial of the former Khmer Rouge prison chief known as Duch resumed in Cambodia on Monday, marking a pivotal moment in the country’s decades-long effort to hold leaders of the brutal regime accountable.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known as Duch, commanded the notorious S-21 security prison in Phnom Penh, where thousands of people were interrogated, tortured and sent to their deaths between 1975 and 1979.

Duch faces charges of crimes against humanity, war crimes, murder and torture before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, a United Nations-backed tribunal established to prosecute senior Khmer Rouge leaders and those considered most responsible for the regime’s atrocities. He has acknowledged overseeing S-21, though the proceedings are intended to determine his full criminal responsibility.

S-21, housed in a former high school and now known as the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, was the center of an extensive detention and interrogation system. An estimated 12,000 to 14,000 men, women and children passed through its gates. Prisoners were photographed, forced to produce confessions—often implicating relatives and colleagues—and subjected to severe torture. Most were later taken to the Choeung Ek killing fields outside Phnom Penh and executed. Only a small number are known to have survived.

Survivors attending the proceedings said the trial revived painful memories but also offered a long-awaited chance for justice.

Chum Mey, who survived S-21 because his mechanical skills were considered useful, has repeatedly described the torture he endured and the loss of his family under the Khmer Rouge. For survivors such as Mey, Duch’s appearance in court represented an opportunity to confront the prison system’s former commander and establish an official record of what happened.

The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, sought to transform Cambodia into an agrarian communist society. Nearly 2 million people are believed to have died from execution, starvation, disease and forced labor during the regime’s rule.

Duch’s case is historically significant because it is the tribunal’s first full trial of a Khmer Rouge official. The proceedings began more than three decades after the regime fell in 1979, following years of political disputes, funding problems and controversy over the court’s structure.

For many Cambodians, the trial is about more than the fate of one defendant. It is a test of whether the country can formally confront one of the darkest chapters in its history—and whether aging survivors will see accountability before it is too late.

counterfactuals.output:
Kaing Guek Eav, better known as **Duch**, was the first senior Khmer Rouge official tried by the U.N.-backed **Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC)**. Prosecutors alleged that, as commandant of the S-21 security prison in Phnom Penh from 1975 to 1979, he created and managed a systematic operation to imprison, torture, extract false confessions from, and ultimately kill perceived enemies of the regime. They said Duch trained interrogators, reviewed confessions, issued orders, and reported to senior Khmer Rouge leaders.

S-21, now the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, held at least **12,000 people—and probably many more**. Prisoners, including Khmer Rouge cadres, civilians, foreigners, women, and children, were photographed, shackled, starved, and tortured through beatings, electric shocks, suffocation, water torture, and other methods. Nearly all were later taken to the Choeung Ek killing fields and executed. Only a handful survived.

Duch faced charges including **crimes against humanity, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, murder, and torture**. Because the tribunal could not impose the death penalty, the maximum possible punishment was **life imprisonment**. He was ultimately convicted and, after appeal, sentenced to life.

The case carried enormous significance for Cambodians because it was the first major courtroom reckoning for crimes committed under the Khmer Rouge, whose rule caused an estimated **1.7 million deaths** through execution, starvation, disease, and forced labor. For survivors and victims’ families, the trial publicly documented what happened, allowed testimony and participation, and challenged decades of impunity. It also had limits: Duch was only one official, many senior leaders had died or remained untried, and some Cambodians felt justice had come far too late.

**Editor’s note:** The draft below is framed around the opening of Kaing Guek Eav’s trial on **Feb. 17, 2009**. Proceedings took place at the U.N.-backed tribunal outside Phnom Penh, while the dateline and scene are from Tuol Sleng, the prison Duch commanded. Quotations should be checked against the tribunal transcript or the original interview recording before publication.

# Cambodia’s first Khmer Rouge defendant goes on trial three decades after Tuol Sleng killings

**By [Reporter Name]**

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia, Feb. 17, 2009** — The rusting beds, shackles and bloodstained photographs remain inside Tuol Sleng, preserved as evidence of a prison where thousands of Cambodians were interrogated and sent to their deaths.

On Tuesday, more than three decades after the Khmer Rouge’s rule ended, the man accused of running that prison became the first senior figure from the regime to face trial.

Kaing Guek Eav, better known as Duch, appeared before a U.N.-backed court on the outskirts of Phnom Penh to answer charges of crimes against humanity and war crimes. Prosecutors say Duch directed a system of detention, torture and execution at Security Prison 21, or S-21, now the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum.

The proceedings mark an unprecedented reckoning in a country where an estimated 1.7 million people died from execution, starvation, forced labor and disease under the Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979.

“This is the first case in the history of this court,” Cambodian co-prosecutor Chea Leang told the judges as the hearing opened.

Duch, a former mathematics teacher who became a meticulous prison administrator, sat behind courtroom glass in a pale shirt, listening through headphones. Now 66, he is accused of overseeing the imprisonment of more than 12,000 people at S-21. Updated archival research has placed the number of documented prisoners even higher.

Only a handful are known to have survived.

The tribunal says prisoners were photographed and forced to write confessions, often after beatings, electric shocks, suffocation and other forms of torture. Many confessed to imaginary plots against the Khmer Rouge leadership. They were then taken to the Choeung Ek killing fields outside Phnom Penh and executed.

International co-prosecutor Robert Petit said the case would establish individual responsibility for a system that turned S-21 into one of the regime’s central killing institutions. Prosecutors allege Duch exercised direct authority over interrogators and guards, approved torture and reported to senior Khmer Rouge leaders.

For survivors, Tuesday’s hearing was less an end than the beginning of an answer they have sought for 30 years.

Chum Mey, one of the few people to emerge alive from S-21, has described being shackled, beaten and subjected to electric shocks during repeated interrogation. Speaking about the long-delayed proceedings, he said simply: “I want justice.”

Another survivor, the artist Vann Nath, later summarized the enduring question at the heart of the case: “I want to know why they did this.”

Vann Nath survived because prison officials used his ability to paint portraits of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot. His paintings of torture inside S-21 now hang in the former prison, confronting visitors with scenes that were never photographed.

At Tuol Sleng on Tuesday, tourists and Cambodian families moved quietly through classrooms converted into cells. Rows of black-and-white prisoner photographs covered the walls: men, women and children staring directly into the camera shortly after arrival. In some pictures, numbered tags hang around their necks.

The stillness of the museum contrasted with the legal arguments unfolding at the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, commonly known as the Khmer Rouge tribunal. The hybrid court combines Cambodian and international judges, prosecutors and law.

Youk Chhang, director of the Documentation Center of Cambodia, which has collected hundreds of thousands of pages of Khmer Rouge records, said the opening of the trial carried significance beyond Duch’s individual fate.

“This is a message to the world that even after 30 years, justice is possible,” Chhang said.

But he and other Cambodian observers warned that no single prosecution could account for the vast scale of the Khmer Rouge disaster. Duch was a prison commander, not a member of the regime’s top political leadership, and many senior figures died before a court could examine their responsibility.

Pol Pot died in 1998 without facing trial. Khmer Rouge military commander Ta Mok died in custody in 2006. Other surviving leaders have been arrested, but their cases are expected to take years.

The tribunal itself has faced criticism over its cost, slow pace and allegations of political interference and corruption. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, himself a former Khmer Rouge cadre who defected, has repeatedly warned against prosecutions that extend too far into the movement’s ranks.

For many victims, however, Duch’s appearance in court broke a silence that had lasted most of their adult lives.

The Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia’s cities after seizing Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975, forcing millions into rural labor camps. Money, markets, religion and private property were abolished. Families were separated, intellectuals and perceived political opponents were hunted, and minor violations could bring imprisonment or death.

S-21 occupied a former high school in the capital. Barbed wire covered the balconies. Classrooms became interrogation rooms and cells. Guards documented prisoners with a bureaucracy that produced mug shots, confessions, execution lists and internal correspondence.

Duch has acknowledged that he headed the prison and has expressed remorse, although the trial will determine the extent of his legal responsibility. His lawyers are expected to argue that he acted under orders and feared he and his family would be killed if he disobeyed.

Prosecutors maintain that the documentary record shows more than passive obedience. They allege Duch trained and supervised staff, selected interrogation methods, reviewed confessions and ensured that prisoners were killed so they could not reveal what had happened inside S-21.

The trial is expected to hear evidence from former guards, historians, experts and survivors. Civil parties — victims participating directly in the proceedings — will also be able to seek collective and moral reparations.

No prison sentence can restore those photographed at Tuol Sleng or erase the decades during which their relatives did not know precisely how they died. The tribunal’s maximum penalty is life imprisonment; Cambodia has no death penalty.

Still, survivors say a public record matters.

At Tuol Sleng, the faces remain fixed on the walls, evidence left behind by the organization that destroyed them. On Tuesday, for the first time, a commander of that organization sat before judges and was required to answer in court.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the background and opening proceedings of Duch’s war-crimes trial, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge death toll, his role as head of S-21, the courtroom atmosphere, and survivors’ responses.
counterfactuals.output:
Cambodia’s first major Khmer Rouge war-crimes trial opened more than three decades after the regime’s 1975–79 rule, during which forced labor, starvation, disease, torture, and execution killed an estimated 1.7 million people—about a quarter of the population.

The defendant, Kaing Guek Eav, better known as Duch, headed the S-21 security prison at Phnom Penh’s Tuol Sleng school. Roughly 14,000–17,000 prisoners were interrogated and tortured there before most were executed at Choeung Ek; only a handful are known to have survived. Prosecutors charged Duch with crimes against humanity and war crimes, alleging that he organized and supervised the prison’s machinery of torture and death.

The opening of the UN-backed tribunal was largely procedural. Duch appeared calm and attentive as judges confirmed his identity and reviewed the charges and court rules. The chamber was crowded with journalists, diplomats, monks, victims’ relatives, and Cambodians who had traveled to witness the long-delayed proceedings. Despite the emotion surrounding the case, the atmosphere was restrained and formal, with tight security and a strong sense of historical significance.

Survivors such as Chum Mey and Bou Meng welcomed the trial as overdue recognition of what happened at S-21. They expressed relief at seeing Duch finally held publicly accountable, while also describing enduring grief and anger over murdered relatives and fellow prisoners. Some wanted a full explanation and genuine remorse more than punishment alone; others felt that no sentence available to the court could match the scale of the crimes.
